title: Three Reasons Classroom Practice Conflicts With Evidence on How Kids Learn
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler asks why decades of cognitive-science findings on spaced practice, interleaving, retrieval and explicit instruction have barely reached classrooms. She sorts the obstacles into three categories: intellectual, because ed schools and professional development ignore or contradict the research; emotional, because teachers fear content is developmentally inappropriate, feel anxious about unfamiliar subjects or resist evidence that their long-used methods fail; and behavioral, because complex daily teaching pulls people back to habit. Her argument is that change must come from both above and below, with teachers understanding the reasons and administrators and policymakers supplying curriculum and coaching. She ends on cautious optimism about knowledge-building curricula at the elementary level.
points: Teacher training emphasizes skills over content and often teaches outdated theory, so many educators never meet the cognitive-science findings.
Experience can mislead: children who seem to read without phonics may be guessing from pictures or memorizing words.
Fears that content is developmentally inappropriate or too hard often mask teachers' own anxiety about unfamiliar subjects.
Even willing teachers revert to ingrained habits, so high-quality curriculum and instructional coaching are needed to sustain change.
Lasting change needs both teacher buy-in and administrator or policy support, since top-down mandates can simply be ignored behind closed doors.
quotes: Cognitive scientists—those who study the learning process—have found that students retain information best through things like spaced practice (distributing learning over a period of time rather than cramming), interleaving (switching between different topics), and retrieval practice (trying to recall information that has been partially forgotten). But few teachers incorporate those practices into their lesson plans or suggest that students use them to study.

But scientists have long known that those kinds of skills can’t be taught directly, in the absence of content. The more information students have on a topic, the better able they are to understand a text about it and think about it critically.
Rather than focusing on recent research, most ed schools teach as gospel theories of child development that academic psychologists consider outdated—like Jean Piaget’s theory of developmental stages.

While teachers’ experience is often valuable, it can also be misleading. For example, to a kindergarten or first-grade teacher it may look as though a child is learning to read without systematic instruction in phonics.

Teaching is an incredibly complex activity. With so many things to juggle, it’s natural to revert to deeply ingrained habits. It’s not impossible for teachers to change their behavior, but it can take time—and support from high-quality curriculum and instructional coaches.

Fundamental change in how and what educators teach can neither be imposed from on high nor spring solely from the grassroots; it has to come from both above and below. When education authorities announce a change in policy without clearly communicating the reasons for it and its value, teachers can simply close their classroom doors and continue to teach in whatever way makes sense to them—as they have done for generations.
